title: AI utilization, modeled output associations, labor mobility, and worker control remain separate evidence stages
source_unit: Deliberately non-pooled task, state-industry, industry-year, executive, establishment, and worker-representation observations
geography: United States, with the NBER executive survey covering the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, and Australia

observations.period: 2026; worker task adoption and exposure comparison

denominator.unit: employed RPS respondents ages 18-64 pooled across August 2025, November 2025, February 2026, and May 2026; companion task analysis has 55,634 worker-task observations

within_task_adoption.value: fewer than half of workers adopt within most occupations and tasks

exposure_explained_variation.unit: adjusted R-squared range across exposure specifications

task_measure_correlations.unit: correlation across worker-survey and public/platform task measures

observations.method: NBER Working Paper 35677 links a representative-style worker survey to detailed occupations and tasks and compares worker-reported adoption with task-exposure and platform chat-log measures.
observations.uncertainty: The RPS is an online survey designed to match key CPS demographics rather than a random sample; task cells, weighting, missingness, and crosswalk versions matter. These are descriptive or predictive comparisons, not causal estimates.
observations.subgroup: Workers, occupations, and task cells; the promoted evidence does not provide a complete demographic or workplace-control table.
observations.counterinterpretation: Shallow or uneven adoption can reflect task fit, access, training, privacy, employer rules, reporting, or classification rather than worker resistance or unequal capability.

observations.period: 2016-2024 outcomes linked to Q2 2025-Q1 2026 AI utilization

denominator.unit: Gallup Workforce Panel worker observations used to construct state-industry utilization; 52,729 in Q2-Q4 2025 and 22,563 in Q1 2026

employment_semielasticity.unit: percent employment difference per 1 percentage-point higher frequent-user share

real_output_semielasticity.unit: percent real-output difference per 1 percentage-point higher frequent-user share

implied_output_change.unit: percent real output as a back-of-envelope implication for a 12-to-24 percentage-point user increase

observations.method: BEA Working Paper 2026-18 links state-by-industry worker-reported frequent AI use to LEHD employment/earnings and BEA real output with state-by-industry and industry-by-year fixed effects; an industry-only BTOS specification is compared.
observations.uncertainty: BEA describes the estimates as descriptive rather than causal. Utilization is measured after much of the outcome window, cells vary in precision, and the industry-only specification does not reproduce the output pattern.
observations.subgroup: US states and two-digit industries, with worker-reported frequent use and employment, earnings, and real-output outcomes.
observations.counterinterpretation: Reverse causality, managerial quality, complementary investment, local demand, and cell composition can produce positive associations without an AI effect; output association does not show who receives the gain.

direct_ai_line_item.value: not currently available in US national accounts

observations.method: BEA Working Paper 2026-8 uses imputation-based difference-in-differences in integrated BEA-BLS industry production accounts, with AI-intensity quartiles based on Census measures.
observations.uncertainty: BEA presents this as early exploratory evidence. Imputation, industry intensity, timing, equal weighting, clustered inference, input-price changes, and unmeasured AI costs limit interpretation.
observations.subgroup: AI-intensive versus other private industries and college/noncollege labor, capital, materials, energy, and services inputs.
observations.counterinterpretation: A lower output-price contribution or labor-share movement can reflect pre-existing differences, demand, input prices, composition, or unmeasured costs; it is not household price pass-through or worker welfare.

observations.period: 2026; executive retrospective and next-three-year expectation survey

denominator.unit: senior business executives at firms in the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, and Australia

no_past_three_year_effect.unit: percent of executives reporting no employment or productivity impact

expected_productivity_change.unit: percent average expected increase at own firm over next three years

expected_employment_change_employers.unit: percent average expected change at own firm

expected_employment_change_employees.unit: percent average expected change at own firm

observations.method: NBER Working Paper 34836 compares current use, retrospective own-firm effects, and forward expectations in a common executive instrument.
observations.uncertainty: Executive perceptions and expectations are not realized administrative outcomes; the sample is not US-only and does not identify occupation, implementation, pay, hours, discretion, or bargaining.
observations.subgroup: Senior executives; reported usage is higher at younger and more productive firms, while employer and employee expectations are distinct perspectives.
observations.counterinterpretation: A retrospective-expectation gap can reflect information, incentives, or definitions rather than realized conflict; projected productivity need not reach workers or households.

denominator.unit: monthly seasonally adjusted total-nonfarm JOLTS rate observations per annual estimate

observations.method: Arithmetic means of BLS seasonally adjusted monthly JOLTS national total-nonfarm rates.
observations.uncertainty: Establishment-survey estimates are subject to sampling error, revisions, seasonal-adjustment updates, and coverage limits; annual rates summarize monthly establishment observations rather than unique workers or AI exposure.
observations.subgroup: Total nonfarm establishments; no occupation, demographic, AI-exposure, or worker-outcome subgroup.
observations.counterinterpretation: Cooling openings and quits may reflect post-reopening normalization, demand, demographics, or sector composition; they are not evidence of AI-induced displacement or a broad loss of bargaining power.

related_sources.claim: NBER task-level worker adoption and exposure evidence.
BEA measurement and early-account context for AI estimates.
NBER executive expectations and retrospective firm effects.

boundary: This is a non-pooled measurement-to-labor-market architecture. It does not establish a causal AI productivity effect, job loss, wage incidence, worker control, household security, cultural meaning, political response, or geopolitical leverage. A same-workplace implementation event with exposure, pay, hours, discretion, appeal, representation, and follow-up remains open.
